summary: A Gentile centurion approaches through Jewish elders and friends, trusting Jesus's command authority without demanding his presence. Jesus marvels at such faith. At Nain, compassion moves Jesus to stop a widow's only son's funeral and restore him, prompting prophetic acclaim. John sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the coming one; Jesus answers with observable signs from Isaiah and then honors John while placing him at a turning point in God's kingdom. Competing audiences reject both John's austerity and Jesus's table fellowship. At a Pharisee's meal, an unnamed woman known as a sinner weeps, anoints Jesus, and receives forgiveness; a creditor parable exposes the host's loveless judgment.
whyItMatters: Faith may appear outside expected boundaries, while a great prophet can ask an anguished question. Luke makes mercy evidential: the sick restored, dead raised, poor evangelized, debt released, and excluded woman sent in peace. Recognition depends less on status than on receiving what God is doing.

context.author: The anonymous writer, traditionally named Luke, joining distinctive Nain and meal stories to shared centurion and John traditions
context.audience: Theophilus and a wider Greek-reading audience, testing faith, prophetic expectation, forgiveness, and social boundary
context.date: Commonly dated around AD 80–90, with earlier and later dates defended
context.setting: Capernaum, Nain's gate and funeral procession, John's inquiry through two disciples, public crowds, and a Pharisee's dining room
context.literaryForm: Healing by delegation, resurrection story, prophetic question and testimony, wisdom saying, meal controversy, and debt parable

outline.heading: Centurion's mediated request and remarkable faith
outline.note: Elders plead for a centurion's dying servant; the centurion sends friends saying 'say the word'; Jesus marvels, and the servant is found well

outline.heading: Widow's only son raised at Nain
outline.note: A widow's only son is carried out dead; Jesus says 'Don't cry', touches the coffin, and says 'arise'; the dead man sits up

outline.heading: John asks; Jesus answers with deeds
outline.note: John's two disciples ask if Jesus is the one coming; he cures many and tells them: the blind see, the dead are raised

outline.heading: Jesus interprets John and this generation
outline.note: Jesus asks what the crowds went to see, calls John 'much more than a prophet', and compares this generation to marketplace children

outline.heading: Woman anoints Jesus; creditor parable and forgiveness
outline.note: A sinful woman wets Jesus's feet with tears, wipes and anoints them; he tells of two debtors and says 'Your sins are forgiven'.

keyVerses.text: When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turned and said to the multitude who followed him, “I tell you, I have not found such great faith, no, not in Israel.”
keyVerses.why: A Gentile officer's trust surprises the story without turning Israel into a rejected caricature.

keyVerses.text: Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John the things which you have seen and heard: that the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them.
keyVerses.why: Jesus answers identity questions through Isaiah-shaped restoration rather than a bare title.

keyVerses.text: He said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”
keyVerses.why: Luke's salvation word gathers forgiveness, restored standing, faith, and peace into one dismissal.

questions.question: Why does the centurion speak through intermediaries?
questions.answer: As an officer he understands delegated authority, and as a Gentile he may show cultural humility about approaching a Jewish healer. Jewish elders commend his support for their synagogue; friends deliver his unworthiness. In Matthew 8:5–8 the centurion speaks to Jesus directly.

questions.question: Does ‘not even in Israel’ insult all Jewish people?
questions.answer: Jesus speaks as a Jew to a largely Jewish following and marvels at one Gentile's exceptional trust. The comparison challenges presumed boundaries but does not say Israel has no faith; Mary, Elizabeth, Simeon, Anna, John, disciples, and crowds already contradict that. Anti-Jewish generalization distorts the scene.

questions.question: Why does Jesus act at Nain before anyone asks?
questions.answer: The widow has lost her only son. Luke says Jesus was moved with compassion. He touches the bier, stops the procession, restores the son, and ‘gave him to his mother,’ echoing Elijah and centering her restoration as well as his life.

questions.question: Does John's question mean he lost all faith?
questions.answer: John, shut in prison since 3:20, hears reports that may not match the fire he announced (3:16–17), and asks honestly whether Jesus is the coming one. Jesus neither shames him nor gives a simple yes; he points to scriptural signs, then publicly calls John more than a prophet. Faith can bring its disorientation to evidence.

questions.question: What does ‘the least in God's Kingdom is greater than John’ mean?
questions.answer: Jesus has just called John the greatest born of women, so on one common reading the next line marks a new salvation-historical position rather than personal contempt. John stands at the threshold announcing the kingdom; those participating in its fulfillment receive a privilege he anticipated. Moral greatness and location in the unfolding story are not the same scale.

questions.question: Who is the woman who anoints Jesus?
questions.answer: Luke does not name her, call her a prostitute, or identify her with Mary Magdalene, Mary of Bethany, or the anointing women in other Gospels. ‘Sinner in the city’ is socially loaded but nonspecific. Centuries of conflation sexualized an unnamed woman beyond the evidence.

questions.question: Is the woman forgiven because she loves much, or does she love because she is forgiven?
questions.answer: The creditor parable makes abundant love the response to large canceled debt, while Jesus's wording can sound causal in English. Readers differ on verse 47: many take it as explaining her acts as evidence of forgiveness; verse 50 names faith, not tears purchased as payment. Grace produces visible love without making love irrelevant.

questions.question: What does ‘your faith has saved you’ hide in English?
questions.answer: The same Greek verb sōzō can mean save, rescue, or make well. Here no physical cure is narrated; forgiveness, peace, and restored relation dominate. In chapter 8 the same line accompanies bodily healing, so Luke intentionally lets salvation span categories English often separates.
